body:
It took me a while to figure out how your scene worked:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/1e8f421a-ce18-4491-9e46-aec54218b165)

Your 'feet' sphere and your 'body' capsule overlap. Since they're connected with a pin joint, they will not collide with each other but they will both collide with the floor (at the same time). The feet have a friction of 0.7, the body has 1.0 (because it has no PhysicsMaterial). When the character touches the floor, friction will be applied to both bodies causing double slow down.

If I disable collision between body and floor then I can see that the vertical velocity at the moment the feet touch the floor is roughly 23, the horizontal velocity roughly 12. The friction model is `MaxFrictionForce = FrictionCoeffiient * NormalForce`, where NormalForce is the force that the body applies to the floor. Using `Impulse = Force * DeltaTime = Mass * DeltaVelocity` and noting that Mass and DeltaTime is the same on both sides we get: MaxDeltaVelocityFriction = FricitionCoefficient * DeltaVelocityVertical (note I'm assuming now that the body can be seen as a point mass which I think is reasonable since the rotation axis are locked). So the maximum expected delta velocity of an object hitting the floor would be: 0.7 * 23 = 16 which is bigger than 12 so the object can stop due to friction in the time step it hits the floor. If I step through the code then that is exactly what happens.

Note that I would avoid using pin joints for these things. It's much cheaper / stable to have a single body with 2 collision shapes or to use only a capsule.

I'm not sure I understand why both frictions are factoring in (**Edit:** ~~well considering the character seems to sink a bit when landing which I thought i already fixed, maybe that's the reason idk~~ just discarded this), when only 1 of the 2 body's surfaces is touching a CollisionShape3D. This is something that wouldn't happen with Unity, even with colliders overlapping.

Maybe a toggle could be added to PinJoint3D so the frictions are separate and only applied for the CollisionShape3D who's friction surface is actually touching another shape?

In any case I'm attempting a revert to the more simple and straightofrward approach of a single body + single collider, as recommended. Because I don't quite see a solution for the previous aproach at the moment, and it at least seems more eficient anyways with a single body as you say.

**Edit:** After a while trying as a single capsule rigidbody I'm already encountering other issues to be expected with friction, since the body can only have one friction I've set to 0.0 so it doesn't stick to walls, it will slide down very low angled ramps easily, or require a hardcoded grounded friction so that the player movement will actually stop. Or maybe I'm just meant to spam physics materials all over the environment collisions at this point to handle proper ground friction... Which actually won't do either unless I very carefully separate the collisions between walls and ground.

I chose the pin joint setup precisely to avoid these shortcomings I find with the suggested single body approach (mainly friction limitations).

Two colliders wouldn't do either since you can't assign different materials to them.

> I'm not sure I understand why both frictions are factoring in

As far as I can see, the feet sphere sticks out approximately 5 cm under your body. With a speed of 23 m/s and an update frequency of 60 Hz you will be moving 23/60 = 0.38 m per frame, so you can penetrate the floor by that amount. This is much more than 5 cm so it is very unlikely that you will only detect collision with the feet, most likely the body capsule will collide in the same step. If you don't want this, you should make the body capsule start much higher (i.e. at least 38 cm + some margin higher).

This will however not fix the problem with the capsule slowing down as a single contact point with 0.7 friction is enough to stop the capsule as the calculations above showed. I think this follows from the laws of physics when using the particular simplified friction model that both Jolt and godot physics use.

I see that the same scene in godot slows down less, but it the pin joint is not completely rigid:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/166a064f-d5b4-4e70-9cea-9803053b0d13)

This could mean that the upper body is slowed down less than it would have if it were completely rigid (speculation, I haven't debugged this).

I can't say much about Unity either as I don't work with it. I think the friction model they use is the same too, but they have a distinction between static and dynamic friction. Dynamic friction is usually lower and would apply in this case, so could be responsible for a difference.

You want your scene to behave non-physically correct and I think it's possible to do that by dynamically updating the friction on the 'feet' (and perhaps also the 'body'). Set the friction to 0 when you're in the air and set it to 0.7 on the frame that you detect ground. This means that the impact will be calculated with 0 friction and will not cause the character to slow down. The next frame you get your normal friction.

> Two colliders wouldn't do either since you can't assign different materials to them.

This is on its way: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/100748
